facts.text: Producer Bruce Newberry bought the Bulldog Drummond rights after reading that Drummond was America's third-favorite fictional character, behind Sherlock Holmes and Tarzan.
Filmink argued this opening, with a seductive assassin staging a mid-air murder, was copied for the opening of the 2000 movie Charlie's Angels.
The Walker Brothers' theme song was co-written by Scott Engel, better known as Scott Walker. It was a small UK hit in October 1966 and is essentially a Scott Walker solo number.
The band Space sampled this song for their hit 'Female of the Species', which played over the closing credits of the first Austin Powers movie.
Italian star Sylva Koscina, who plays Penelope, was dubbed by voice artist Nikki Van der Zyl. Koscina had also been considered for Tatiana in From Russia with Love.
Star Richard Johnson (Hugh Drummond) was director Terence Young's first choice to play James Bond in Dr. No (1962). He got a Bond-style spy hero here instead.
The title comes from Rudyard Kipling's 1911 poem 'The Female of the Species'. It also echoes author Sapper's Drummond novel of that name, filmed as Bulldog Drummond Comes Back (1937).
Leonard Rossiter, who plays board member Henry Bridgenorth, later became TV's Rupert Rigsby in Rising Damp and Reginald Perrin. He also had a speaking part in Kubrick's 2001.
Elke Sommer, playing assassin Irma Eckman, was paid $170,000 for the role.
Steve Carlson, who plays Drummond's nephew Robert, made his movie debut here, according to The Magnificent 60s.
British censors worried about the murder of board member Henry Bridgenorth. The producers fought the censors over the film's women assassins, torture and promiscuity.
Elke Sommer was Playboy's October 1964 cover girl. Unhappy with the roles she got after this film, she posed nude for the magazine again in December 1967.
Sylva Koscina (Penelope) first became an international name as Iole, bride of Steve Reeves' muscleman hero in the Italian sword-and-sandal hit Hercules (1958).
Director Ralph Thomas admitted he made this for 'greed': three months, lots of money, a great location, and a lot of fun.
Screenwriter Jimmy Sangster tried for a star Drummond: Stanley Baker, Peter O'Toole, Jack Hawkins, Stephen Boyd and David Niven were discussed, with Australian Rod Taylor the favorite.
Co-writer Jimmy Sangster was on a break from Hammer Films, where he'd written The Curse of Frankenstein (1957), Dracula (1958) and The Mummy (1959).
Star Nigel Green had played Nayland Smith in The Face of Fu Manchu (1965). Later in this film Drummond mocks a character with a Fu Manchu jibe.
At the Rome Film Festival, Quentin Tarantino revealed this was the first film he remembers seeing. He was five years old.
Screenwriting was a team job: Jimmy Sangster, David D. Osborn (who also wrote Maroc 7) and Liz Charles-Williams, for whom this was her screen debut.
Its X rating from the British censors was for the brutality and promiscuity of its two female villains. One review says it could air on regular TV now.
Hugh Drummond is never called 'Bulldog' in this movie, apparently because the nickname seemed wrong for the Swinging Sixties. Here Boxer calls him 'Dog' once.
In the novels Drummond was a World War I veteran. Here he is updated to a Korean War veteran, hence the Korea tunnel reference.
Director Ralph Thomas, famous for the Doctor in the House comedies, had already tried a Bond spoof with Agent 8¾ (1964), a background that arguably gave this film's action extra punch.
Richard Johnson said of his Drummond: 'I couldn't respect the man. He was bigoted and brutal.' He played a braver, more physical version of himself instead.
The film was Amerlon Productions' first, a subsidiary of Inflight, the company that showed in-flight movies. Rank Organisation provided the financing; its budget is listed at about 1.7 million.
The film was announced in 1964 as Female of the Species, part of a Rank Organisation slate of eight films worth £4.5 million. Shooting didn't start until 1966.
When Rank announced its 1966 slate, this Drummond thriller sat alongside The Quiller Memorandum, Maroc 7, The Long Duel and The Battle of Britain.
Filming began 23 May 1966 in Technicolor and Techniscope, with interiors at Pinewood Studios and the Italian coast scenes shot at Lerici and La Spezia.
The Monthly Film Bulletin sniffed that the film 'succeeds only in giving it the look of a poor imitation', adding 'the original Drummond would have found the whole thing rather distasteful.'
Drummond's Lloyd's insurance job is a leftover of writer Jimmy Sangster's 1964 plan: a rich Mayfair Drummond working as a Lloyd's underwriter who travels the world.
Virginia North made her film debut here. She went on to become a Bond girl in On Her Majesty's Secret Service.
Nigel Green (Carl Petersen) really served in Korea, like Drummond in this film. He suffered a head wound that needed a metal skull plate, and battled depression and headaches for life.
Milton Reid, who plays henchman Chang, was a pro wrestler known as The Mighty Chang. He reportedly challenged Harold Sakata to a shoot match over the Oddjob role in Goldfinger.
Suzanna Leigh (Grace) was the goddaughter of Vivien Leigh, and took her screen surname from her.
Director Ralph Thomas said the film was meant as a pilot for a TV series. In 1964 writer Jimmy Sangster had talked of three Drummond films plus a series.
Richard Johnson returned as Drummond in the 1969 sequel Some Girls Do. The two films were later released together as a DVD double feature.
Suzanna Leigh (Grace) later played Harry Nilsson's love interest in the rock-and-roll horror comedy Son of Dracula (1974), starring Ringo Starr.
In the sequel Some Girls Do (1969), Joanna Lumley appears uncredited as a robot. Filmink judged it 'far less fun' than this film, and Monthly Film Bulletin called it an 'inane sequel'.
The giant chess pieces are loosely based on the 12th-century Lewis Chessmen found in Scotland in 1831. After filming they sat in Pinewood's grounds and were repainted for years.
Those oversized chess pieces were reused in UFO's 'Timelash', Sleuth (1974), The Man with the Golden Gun (1974) and The Sweeney, before vanishing in the late 1990s.
Elke Sommer later won a $3.3 million libel judgment in 1993 against Zsa Zsa Gabor, after a feud that began in 1984.
